result:
Right now, as you read this, the Moon is slipping away from us. Not dramatically—it moves about 3.8 centimeters per year, roughly the rate at which fingernails grow. But the fact remains: the Moon is leaving.

Billions of years ago, it hung much closer, so close that Earth's days lasted only a few hours. The tides it raised on our young planet were monstrous, and those tides did something subtle and strange. They transferred energy. The Earth's rotation slowed, and the Moon, absorbing that borrowed momentum, drifted outward. We've been in this slow dance ever since—a separation so gradual that no human lifetime can perceive it, yet so relentless it has reshaped the length of every day since the Earth was young.

One day, far in the future, the Moon will appear smaller in our sky. Total solar eclipses will become impossible; the Moon's disk will no longer cover the Sun. Future civilizations—if they exist—will never know the strange coincidence we enjoy now, that our Moon and our Sun appear almost exactly the same size, allowing that perfect, chilling corona to ring the darkness.

I find this oddly moving. We live in a brief window of cosmic geometry, a moment when the heavens align just so. The eclipses our ancestors watched with terror and awe were a temporary gift, a coincidence of scale and distance. Nothing about it was permanent. Even the sky is a passing phase.

The Moon is leaving. Notice it while it lasts.
